## Before the bench {.center}

### Where S1 left off

S1 fed the converter a **constant** and found about 11 effective bits out of a
nominal 16.

A constant does not care *when* you sample it. So S1 could not see:

- the sample-and-hold closing at a slightly random instant;
- the board's oscillator running fast or slow;
- what it costs to assume the samples are evenly spaced.

Today the input moves, and all three become visible.

### The one-line reason

$$
\dot{V}_\max = 2\pi f A
$$

A timing error of $\Delta t$ becomes an amplitude error of
$\dot{V}\,\Delta t$ — and the slope grows with frequency.

The same 10 µs of timing error costs **ten times as much** at 1 kHz as at
100 Hz.

## At the bench {.center}

### What you will do

1. Find the sampling rate the board **actually** achieves.
2. Set the generator to about 90 % of full scale — and check it at the pin.
3. Sweep the frequency over two decades, recording ~2000 samples each time.
4. Fit a sinusoid to each record, twice: on the nominal grid, and on `t_us`.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Two ways to waste the session

**Clipping.** A few clipped codes at the peaks wreck the fit. Verify the
headroom at the pin before the first recording, and do not touch the
amplitude again.

**Using the board's own DAC as the source.** Its errors are correlated with
the ADC's, so they cancel. The result looks excellent and means nothing.
:::

### Then

Open [the handbook](handbook.qmd) for the full procedure, and one of the two
analysis templates — [Python](analysis-py.qmd) or [R](analysis-r.qmd).

Both ship with reference data covering the whole sweep, so you can read the
entire analysis before touching the generator.

## What you should come away with {.center}

### Three sentences you should be able to defend

1. "This board delivers $x$ effective bits at $f_1$ and $y$ at $f_2$, measured
   by sine fit against its own timestamps."
2. "Analysing the same samples on the nominal grid instead costs $z$ bits —
   which is what timestamping is worth."
3. "Below $f_c$ the converter is noise limited and a quieter front end would
   help; above it, it is jitter limited and only a better clock would."

### And one number for the rest of the course

The crossover frequency. It decides whether an improvement to *any* later
measurement on this platform is worth making.
